title: one-day-skim-inference-ops-cliffnotes-benji-2026-09-12
body:
Context: one-day skim of talks / posters / hallway convos at the regional InferenceOps meetup (2026-09). Notes are messy — meant to capture ideas I want to prototype next sprint and a short reading list. Took public-paper links where available, otherwise shorthand.

Top-level takeaways (TL;DR):
- Practical wins come from small ops-level tricks: adaptive prefix caching, sequence-length-aware batching, and cheap KV compression for long-chunk workloads. Not a single magic model change.
- Quantization still good for cost but expect brittle outliers (rare hallucination/formatting corruption) — need unit tests / evals per prompt set.
- Tail latency matters more than mean for customer experience; invest in fallback routing + fast-subset models.

Paper / talk snippets (quick)
1) "Adaptive prefix cache for conversational workloads" (poster) — idea: cache partial KV states keyed by conversational turns + cheap similarity to avoid full recompute for repeated patterns.
   Quick notes: store compressed snapshots every N turns; when request arrives compute cheap fingerprint and splice in cache with delta reforward.
   Why it matters to Redwood: reduces per-token compute for repetitive multi-turn apps (support chat, agent state). Could pair with our existing prefix/KV caching layer.
   Quick experiment: run a replay of last 7 days of chat logs for two customers (low and high entropy) and measure token-ops saved vs cache hit heuristics (fingerprint threshold).

2) "Length-aware batching heuristics" (talk + slides) — packs by predicted generation length rather than input length; schedules small fast buckets for low-latency paths.
   Insight: majority of requests are short tails; naive batching hurts latency.
   Why Redwood: ties directly to Dedicated autoscaler and per-route SLOs; could be a policy option in runtime: latency-first vs throughput-first.
   Quick experiment: simulator + traces; implement greedy pack-by-pred-length in our batcher and compare tail p95/p99 latencies.

3) "Tiny-KV compression: lossy delta encoding for KV caches" (paper) — lossy compression with controlled error; decompress + local correction step using small attention.
   Notes: tradeoff quantized KV size vs small extra attention to correct noise. Good for long-context RAG-like flows.
   Redwood angle: reduce GPU memory footprint per replica and increase effective context capacity or reduce shard count.
   Experiment: modify KV serialization in the runtime to support 4-bit delta + corrective micro-attention on read; bench memory and quality on long doc summarization evals.

4) "Quantization failure modes" (panel) — group looked at corner cases where int8/int4 changes tokenization-like artifacts (bad punctuation, numeric truncation). Recommendation: add small synthetic tests that exercise numeric formatting and structured output after quantization.
   Action: add a quantization smoke-test suite that runs against production prompt-set samples and checks for deterministic fields (dates, LLM-JSON keys).

Operational ideas raised in hallway convos
- Canary routing at invocation level: route small percentage of live traffic to quantized variant + monitor structured-output regressions (per-prompt checks). Works better than spike-testing offline.
- Smart fallback chains: fast tiny model -> medium model -> large model (cost-aware SLOs). Useful when Dedicated bursts exceed capacity.
- Per-tenant cache warming: prefetch likely prefixes for heavy customers during business hours.

Personal todo / shortlist (things I want to pick up)
- [ ] Prototype length-aware packer in local batcher sim (Benji) — first pass: greedy algorithm that packs by predicted output tokens. Instrument p50/p95/p99.
- [ ] Add 6 synthetic structured-output tests to quant-smoke suite (dates, currency, JSON keys, UUID format, phone numbers, list cardinality). (pair with Asha).
- [ ] Build small replay harness to test adaptive prefix caching heuristics using anonymized customer chat logs (Kendra assist on data pull).
- [ ] Spike a KV-delta-compress prototype (Python export/import hook) and run memory / clamp-quality tests on summarization traces.

Notes-to-self: design constraints and guardrails
- Any cache/compression approach must preserve privacy: encrypted at rest and never write raw unredacted logs to shared buckets. For the replay harness, use tokenized and redacted traces.
- Keep canary window small (1–2% traffic for initial trials) and automate rollback when structured-output errors exceed 0.5% over baseline.

Short reading list (links I pulled)
- "Efficient Inference with KV Compression" — arXiv (linked above).
- "Batching and Scheduling for Low-Latency LLMs" — workshop slides (save).
- "Quantization: Practical Guide and Failure Modes" — systems blog post (internal).

Open questions
- How to set fingerprint threshold for adaptive prefix cache in a way that generalizes across tenants? (learned threshold per-tenant?)
- Can we derive predicted generation length cheaply and reliably from the prompt in <1 ms? (model-lite classifier?)
- Is corrective micro-attention on compressed KV reads cost-effective vs keeping larger memory footprint?

Ideas for next sync (agenda bullets)
- Quick 10 min on length-aware batching sim results + decision: add as opt-in runtime policy?
- Demo of quant-smoke tests and proposed canary flow (Asha)
- Discuss data access plan for chat replay (privacy checklist and Kendra's redaction plan)

Misc stray thoughts / half-baked
- Maybe we can expose an opt-in "sticky-prefix" feature for customers who want cheaper multi-turn pricing — they accept some heuristics on prefix reuse and an SLA tradeoff.
- Consider a metric for "effective context capacity" that counts compressed KVs weighted by expected correction cost — easier to communicate tradeoffs to customers.

End.

(If I don't action these in 2 weeks, ping me @ slack)
